question: Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste became applicable on 12 August 2026. The following day, at a press conference, a senior official at the Commission told the German daily newspaper Die Welt: ‘We encourage Member States not to apply the new rules and not to impose penalties’, calling the text ‘clearly disproportionate’1.

At the same time, French ecommerce microenterprises have warned about the red tape, including as regards apostilles and the costs imposed2 for representation in each country. Those costs can exceed EUR 600 – and even EUR 2 000 – per country per year for companies with minimal turnover, forcing them to cease operations in several European countries.

On 24 June 2026, due to the lack of a majority, the Council supposedly abandoned the proposal to suspend Article 45(3) of the regulation. An exemption for small businesses will be debated in the European Parliament in October3. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that the ‘pragmatic approach’ recommended by the Commission official means that no fines should be imposed and clarify whether the instructions to not apply the regulation have been formalised in writing to the national supervisory authorities?

Has the Commission made written representations to major intermediaries, such as Amazon, to confirm that this ‘pragmatic approach’ is actually applied in their dealings with small European businesses?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) The Commission is aware that the costs and administrative burden for selling relatively small quantities across several Member States can be significant for small businesses.

To minimise administrative burdens and costs for small businesses, the Commission proposed as priority action in its Environmental Omnibus1, to suspend the obligation for producers to appoint an authorised representative when they sell packaged products directly to consumers in Member States other than the one where they are located.

The proposal is currently being examined by the European Parliament and the Council. In the meantime, the Commission recommended to Member States to take a constructive and pragmatic approach, to avoid disproportionate implementation and clarified that the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)2 does not establish financial sanctions in case of non-compliance with the extended producer responsibility rules.

Chapter XVI of the updated Frequently Asked Questions document3 contains more details about the issue. The Commission can only provide guidance to the Member States how to enforce the PPWR rules, as the competence is with them.

Moreover, the Commission encouraged Member States to make use of the national flexibilities they have to avoid disproportionate regulatory burden on producers, including small and medium-sized enterprises, of small quantities of packaging, in line with the Waste Framework Directive and the PPWR4.

legislation_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste, amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and Directive (EU) 2019/904, and repealing Directive 94/62/EC, OJ L, 2025/40, 22.1.2025. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/faq-packaging-and-packaging-waste-regulation-ppwr_en.

4 Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives (‘Member States shall ensure equal treatment of producers of products regardless of their origin or size, without placing a disproportionate regulatory burden on producers, including small and medium-sized enterprises, of small quantities of products") and Regulation (EU) 2025/40 ("Producer responsibility organisations shall ensure equal treatment of producers regardless of their origin or size, without placing a disproportionate burden on producers of small quantities of packaging, including packaging of packaged products, including small and medium-sized enterprises’).
